statements.quote:
The dataset of story ideas with their creativity ratings used for fine-
tuning the ML models is available at: https://osf.io/rm4cz/?view_only=
ac999ab27fd34f6ab4de5bf1c957d92a
statements.locator: p. 3, footnote 3. PDF line breaks retained; the URL continues onto the next line.

statements.quote: We started by conducting a study with a wizard-ed robot to collect storytelling data with children. We used this data in our second study to develop an autonomous robotic system capable of collaboratively telling stories with children and report on the results of evaluating it.
statements.locator: p. 4, Section 2.2 (Social robots for collaborative storytelling); provenance of the model-training data.

statements.quote: To generate the behavior of the robot, the tele-operator randomly chose from a pool of ideas that was extracted from a storytelling dataset previously collected with children who used the same software (Elgarf et al., 2022a; Elgarf et al., 2021a).
statements.locator: p. 5, Section 3.2.2.2 (Experimental design); source of Study 1 robot story ideas.

statements.quote: For more details about the design of the study and the story ideas used, please refer to Elgarf et al. (2021b).
statements.locator: p. 5, Section 3.2.2.2; reference for Study 1 design and materials.

statements.quote:
For simplicity and consistency,
we implemented a software interface to aid the child in generating
ideas. The software interface had a castle theme, several scenes,
4 characters, and 9 objects to choose from in order to tell
the story. Figure 1 displays the setup of the interaction and the details
of the storytelling software.
statements.locator: p. 5, Section 3.2.2.2; description of the study software. PDF line breaks retained.

statements.quote: Then we assessed children’s fluency and originality of ideas through behavioral coding analysis using the ELAN software[4] (Wittenburg et al., 2006).
statements.locator: p. 6, Section 3.2.4 (Measures); ELAN software is linked in footnote 4, also repeated on p. 10.

statements.quote: We used training data provided from a previously collected dataset Elgarf et al. (2021a), Elgarf et al. (2021b) of child-robot interactions in a storytelling context using the same storytelling software that we are using in this research. We extracted children’s story ideas from the dataset and labeled them as creative versus non-creative ideas according to a creativity score.
statements.locator: p. 7, Section 3.3 (The creative and non-creative ML models); provenance and labeling of training statements.

statements.quote: For more details about the training and assessment process of our ML models, please refer to Elgarf and Peters (2022).
statements.locator: p. 8, Section 3.3; reference for model training and assessment.

statements.quote: For more details about the design of the study and the robot’s cognitive behavior, please refer to Elgarf et al. (2022b).
statements.locator: p. 8, Section 3.4.2.2; reference for Study 2 design and robot behavior.

statements.quote: A couple of weeks before the study, consent forms allowing the children’s participation in the study, the data collection and the publishing of the data were sent to the children’s parents for their signature.
statements.locator: p. 8, Section 3.4.3 (Procedures); consent for data collection and publication.

statements.quote:
The raw data supporting the conclusions of this article will be
made available by the authors, without undue reservation.
statements.locator: p. 13, Data availability statement. PDF line breaks retained.

statements.quote: Written informed consent was obtained from the minor(s)’ legal guardian/next of kin for the publication of any potentially identifiable images or data included in this article.
statements.locator: p. 13, Ethics statement; consent for publication of identifiable images or data.

deposits.notes: This is the same URL recorded in forms/c298.json. OSF calls the project Fostering Children's Creativity through Collaborative Storytelling with a Social Robot and describes it as supplementary materials for the 2024 Frontiers submission; the wiki matches this paper's two studies. The landing page, node metadata, OSF-storage listing, children listing, provider listing and wiki returned HTTP 200. The storage listing has exactly two files, no pagination, one storage provider and zero child nodes. The token-free node endpoint https://api.osf.io/v2/nodes/rm4cz/ also returned HTTP 200 with public=true; no account is needed. Both XLSX files were downloaded and read in memory, with HTTP 200 at https://osf.io/download/vj8gt/?view_only=ac999ab27fd34f6ab4de5bf1c957d92a and https://osf.io/download/6mzyf/?view_only=ac999ab27fd34f6ab4de5bf1c957d92a. The first workbook has 14 worksheets; the second has 13. rows_checked=640 counts numbered story statements (IDs 1 through 640) in the first workbook's Statements sheet, excluding the header, notes and summary/formula-only rows. These are statement IDs, not child IDs. The Prompts sheet has 636 numbered statements after four repeated statements are removed; its columns are #, Completion, Total Creativity score normalised, Prompt. The Prompts 2 sheet contains the same 636 classified examples (439 Non-creative, 197 Creative). These labels classify training content, not experimental assignment. Separate creative and non-creative training sheets each contain 197 statement texts. Other sheets concern pilot survey administration, vouchers, attention checks and drafting; their ID fields do not link these story statements to the children in S1/S2. has_outcome_scores=true refers only to statement-level training creativity scores, not study participants' outcome scores. has_texts_or_ideas=true refers to training statements. Classified as materials_only because these are model-training materials rather than released S1/S2 analysis data. Section 3.3 cites earlier source datasets, including the S1 report, but no statement-to-child, source-study or experimental-arm mapping is provided, so S1 coverage cannot be established and no S2 participant output is confirmed. No analysis code, model weights or trial transcripts linked to participant IDs were found. The repository supplies no license (node_license=null); the article's CC BY license is not assumed to license the deposit.

deposits.notes: Related candidate inspected and EXCLUDED as participant data for c298. DataCite's Elgarf search returned DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/7NQ3E; the verified author's public OSF projects also list it. The project is explicitly for the HRI 2022 paper 'And then what happens?' Promoting Children's Verbal Creativity Using a Robot, cited by c298 as Elgarf et al. (2022a), a source of earlier story ideas. It is not the Once upon a story (S1) or CreativeBot (S2) experiment. The landing page, metadata, OSF-storage listing, storage-provider listing and children listing returned HTTP 200; one storage provider, eight files and zero child nodes were listed without pagination. All eight spreadsheets were downloaded and inspected in memory (HTTP 200). Raw data - Verbal creative process - Children.xlsx, sheet Data storytelling, has two header rows followed by 68 participant-ID rows, with 35 Promotion and 33 Prevention labels; 58 rows contain pre and post fluency values. These are observed spreadsheet record counts, not analyzed counts for this paper. Descriptive statistics for raw data.xlsx repeats those earlier-study records and includes derived summaries/analyses. The other files contain coding rules, coding schemes, robot scripts and scene descriptions. The arm and score flags describe this OTHER study's actual data and must not be used to mark c298 public_participant_data. studies_covered=[] means no matching study from forms/c298.json. No participant story transcripts are provided; the text in materials consists of robot stimuli, coding examples and scene descriptions, hence has_texts_or_ideas=false for participant outputs. License verified through the node's license relationship at https://api.osf.io/v2/licenses/563c1cf88c5e4a3877f9e96a/ (HTTP 200).

notes: Checked 2026-10-09 using Python urllib with User-Agent atlas-screening/0.1 and no login, access request or personal contact identifier. Read the complete 83,443-character markdown conversion, including the end matter and references, and checked the relevant PDF text in the 15-page version of record. There are no appendices, preregistration links or separate supplementary-file statements in that document; the sole study-specific repository link is footnote 3. The two explicit availability statements are quoted from the PDF with original line breaks. Public_partial refers only to the publicly readable ancillary training statements and their scores. No public participant dataset usable for the c298 experiments S1/S2 was confirmed. The second deposit is retained as an audited, excluded search lead, not as evidence that c298 participant data are available. The training files do not provide child identifiers, assignments or participant outcome summaries; their creative/non-creative labels must not be treated as study arms. They could support descriptive diversity analyses of the training pool only, not by-arm diversity of children's outputs from either study. We therefore cannot compute the requested participant-based means, SDs, SEs, analyzed counts or arm-specific output diversity from these deposits. The paper's p. 13 statement promises that authors will make raw data available but does not literally say 'on request', supply a participant-data download, or establish any access procedure; author-mediated availability is therefore recorded without claiming access was obtained. The supplied screening form has no final key or final.open_items field, and open_questions is empty; what_we_could_compute is null rather than an invented list of open items. The form's studies and outcome descriptions were used to identify the intended data needs. The form also does not establish random assignment for either study; this check does not change that eligibility assessment. All four required repository APIs were searched by the full title and Elgarf, and the OSF title variants and verified author's projects were additionally checked. All successful searches returned HTTP 200; the two initial Zenodo HTTP 400 errors were resolved by reducing page size to its unauthenticated maximum, without authentication. No GitHub repository or other data-repository link was named, so no GitHub API quota was used. Additional explicit paper-link checks: https://ankicozmorobot.com/ returned HTTP 200; https://beta.openai.com/ returned HTTP 403 and was not pursued; https://archive.mpi.nl/tla/elan failed TLS certificate verification, so HTTP status is null (not inferred dead). These are general product/software links, not deposits of this paper's data. https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2024.1457429 returned HTTP 200 and redirected to the publisher's full article; that page also returned HTTP 200 and exposed no separate supplementary data attachments. Only the requested output JSON is written; all remote spreadsheets were read in memory.
